reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents beginner-oriented Adobe Illustrator instruction and ordinary ways to monetize design skills through photo banks, print shops, font marketplaces, and Etsy-style products. The speaker describes personal photo-bank income and uploading designs as personal experience and suggested work distribution, without a guarantee of viewer returns or a deceptive participation flow.

photo banks don't have exams and you can upload your work immediately after you sign up and start to sell your designs.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the sequence the viewer is given: the speaker reports that photo banks remain a source of income for her, at about seven to eight hundred euros, then says viewers can sign up, upload work immediately, and start selling designs. The description also supplies links to her stock portfolios. Those elements make the income figure more than background biography: it gives the proposed sign-up and upload action a concrete monetary appeal. The video does not establish that a new contributor can earn anything comparable, yet her result is presented alongside a low-friction path to participation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls the earnings personal experience, but that does not explain their placement next to the invitation to sign up and start selling. Nor does saying the viewer must upload designs resolve the concern: the speaker explicitly presents the process as open to beginners without an exam. The defense identifies no evidence that her stated income is representative of what a beginner can achieve.

citations.quote: photo banks don't have exams and you can upload your work immediately after you sign up and start to sell your designs.
photo bumps still one of mine incomes about seven to eight hundred euros

true_side_reply.rebuttal: An account of one designer's income is not a promise of the same income to viewers. The proposed action is uploading one's own work for sale, not claiming a payment for signing up. Her account also says she spent about five years earning through photo banks and has thousands of designs on stock sites. That context makes the result dependent on sustained creative work, not a low-effort reward.

citations.quote: About first 5 years of my designing career, I have been earning money only on photobanks.
I have more than 10000 designs on Adobe stock and 6000 designs 6,000 designs on Shutterstock.

opening.argument: The concern is the combination of signals, not the mere mention of design work. The speaker pairs a personal figure of seven to eight hundred euros with the claim that beginners can sign up and upload immediately, without an exam. The description then offers direct portfolio links. A viewer can reasonably read that combination as an accessible income opportunity endorsed by a claimed successful participant. The evidence does not show that the quoted earnings are typical, or that immediate access translates into sales; those missing qualifications matter when ease of entry and a specific income figure are presented together.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that selling designs requires work, but its own evidence does not show how likely a beginner is to make sales. The speaker's claim that photo banks have no exams establishes ease of access, not a likely return. Pairing that access with her income figure can still create a misleading expectation without an explicit guarantee.

citations.quote: photo banks don't have exams and you can upload your work immediately after you sign up and start to sell your designs.
photo bumps still one of mine incomes about seven to eight hundred euros

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The opening identifies an expectation a viewer might form, but cites no promise that signing up yields earnings or that the speaker's income is typical. Immediate uploading concerns access to a marketplace; the work still has to sell. Elsewhere the speaker says marketplace sales require strong Illustrator skills, reinforcing that the video discusses making and selling creative work rather than obtaining an easy payment.

citations.quote: you can upload your work immediately after you sign up and start to sell your designs.
If you want to sell your designs of your marketplaces, you need to have strong skills in Adobe

opening.argument: The instructional framing also serves a promotional function. The speaker says she teaches Illustrator, but this video directs attention to ways to earn money, names selling venues, and points viewers to links beneath the video. For photo banks, she presents her own earnings and tells viewers they can sign up and start selling designs immediately. Judge the practical effect of that sequence: it moves the audience from learning a tool toward joining an external selling platform, with a personal income claim supplying the incentive. The educational setting does not, by itself, answer whether that income-led invitation is misleading.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense describes a lesson about distributing work, but the speaker also gives viewers a participation path: sign up, upload, and sell, with links to her profiles below. Calling that educational does not make the income claim incidental. The defense's cited work requirement explains what users would upload; it does not establish that the speaker's earnings are a sound basis for expecting returns.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Discussing where artists can sell their work does not turn a tutorial into a deceptive solicitation. The speaker describes several distinct outlets, including print shops where buyers decide whether to purchase a design and Etsy listings that require a whole product. The opening identifies no claim that following her links produces income. Its promotional reading leaves out the central condition throughout the video: viewers must create something buyers want.
